title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite, eternal, and full of stars, why isn't every point in the night sky blazing with light?
summary: A simple observation — that the night sky is dark rather than a wall of light — turns out to encode deep facts about the age, size, and history of the universe.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. Between the stars, there is darkness. This seems too obvious to need explaining — of course space is mostly empty and dark. But in the 1800s, the astronomer Heinrich Olbers pointed out that under a very natural set of assumptions, the night sky should not be dark at all. It should be a blazing, uniform wall of light, as bright as the surface of the sun, in every direction you look.

The Naive Argument

Suppose the universe is infinite in extent, eternal in age, and roughly uniformly filled with stars. Pick any direction to look. Your line of sight eventually has to hit a star — because with infinitely many stars scattered through infinite space, there is no direction where the line just misses everything forever. A star twice as far away looks a quarter as bright, but there are also four times as many stars at that distance in a given angular slice of sky. Those two effects exactly cancel. So every patch of sky, however small, should on average be as bright as a stellar surface. The whole sky should glow like the sun, day and night.

Obviously it doesn't. Something in the assumptions is wrong.

Resolving the Paradox

The resolution isn't that space is too empty — it's that the universe is not infinite in age. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, and light travels at a finite speed. That means we can only ever see stars whose light has had time to reach us: a sphere roughly 13.8 billion light-years in radius (larger once you account for cosmic expansion). Beyond that boundary, there may be more stars, but their light simply hasn't arrived yet. The sky is dark because the universe has a finite age, not because it lacks stars.

Cosmic expansion compounds this. Light from the most distant visible objects has been redshifted by the stretching of space itself, shifting much of that ancient light out of the visible spectrum entirely and into microwaves — which is exactly what we detect as the cosmic microwave background, the actual (very faint, very cold) afterglow of the early universe. In a sense, Olbers was almost right: the sky IS glowing everywhere, uniformly, at every wavelength. It's just glowing in microwaves at 2.7 kelvin instead of visible light at thousands of degrees, because the universe has been expanding and cooling for billions of years.

Why a Simple Observation Runs So Deep

What makes Olbers' paradox remarkable is how much cosmology it forces out of one everyday fact. Before general relativity, before Hubble measured galactic redshifts, before the Big Bang model existed, the mere darkness of the night sky was already evidence that the universe could not be infinite, static, and eternal all at once — at least one of those had to give. It took over a century for astronomers to figure out which one: not infinite space, but finite time. A backyard observation, taken seriously and followed to its logical end, anticipated one of the twentieth century's biggest discoveries.

Where It Still Gets Strange

Even today, the paradox raises live questions. We don't actually know if space itself is infinite — only that the observable universe, the part whose light has reached us, is finite. If space is truly infinite and stars go on forever beyond our cosmic horizon, then in principle the "unseen" universe already satisfies Olbers' original nightmare — it's just perpetually, permanently out of view, hidden behind a wall of time rather than distance.

perspectives.title: Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is resolved observationally: the darkness of the sky combined with the cosmic microwave background gives direct evidence for a universe with a finite, measurable age.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: Expansion redshifts ancient starlight out of the visible band entirely, converting what would have been blinding light into the faint microwave background we detect today.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler used the same dark-sky observation in 1610 to argue the universe must be finite, centuries before the tools existed to actually test that idea.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' paradox is a textbook case of a thought experiment forcing a hidden assumption into the open — showing that even 'obvious' premises like an eternal universe can be quietly false.
